comparison: Perfect alignment on Experiment 3 findings (C101-C106, C117, C160). Both evaluations find the evidence convincing that baseline relationships constrain adaptation patterns, with OpenEval providing detailed statistical validation and peer reviewers accepting these findings as supporting the theoretical framework.

Strong agreement on baseline stereotypical relationship findings (C5, C48-C59, C114, C119-C120). Both find the evidence well-supported through statistical analyses and kinematic data. OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor while peer reviewers accept findings without challenge, noting the optimization interpretation.

Agreement on Experiment 1 adaptation findings (C63-C72, C115, C129-C130). Both accept that adaptation follows baseline relationships. Peer Reviewer 1 requests clearer presentation of time course data, suggesting presentation improvements rather than questioning core findings, while OpenEval finds evidence fully supported.

Strong agreement on task design and methodology (C4, C37-C46, C123-C125). All peer reviewers explicitly praised the novel task design as innovative and fruitful. OpenEval confirms comprehensive methodological documentation. Both evaluations find this aspect well-supported.

Agreement on main theoretical conclusions (C11-C12, C174-C175). Both find the dual role of baseline relationships (control and adaptation) to be a valuable theoretical contribution. Peer Reviewer 1 suggests clarifying the abstract's final sentence for theoretical impact, while OpenEval notes some mechanistic details remain interpretive.

Partial overlap on Experiment 2 findings. OpenEval R6 addresses statistical validation of end-effector irrelevant perturbations (C78-C89), while peer R4 focuses on the theoretical significance of task-irrelevant perturbations causing task-relevant errors (C85-C93, C116, C146, C155). Both find evidence convincing but peer reviewers request more discussion of underlying mechanisms.

Partial overlap on Experiment 2 error findings. OpenEval R7 addresses end-effector relevant errors from irrelevant adaptation (C90-C94, C155-C158) with detailed statistical support. Peer R4 acknowledges this as an important novel finding but requests more theoretical discussion of why adaptation occurs and how internal models explain it.

Both address synthesis of dual mechanisms (C95, C116). OpenEval finds the synthesis logical and well-supported by experimental data. Peer reviewers accept this as valuable theoretical contribution showing how baseline relationships determine learning, with editor confirming evidence is convincing.

Both address mechanistic interpretations (C146-C149, C163-C168). OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN, noting they are explicitly speculative and not directly tested. Peer reviewers similarly express uncertainty, requesting extended discussion of how internal models may explain the findings, particularly for end-effector irrelevant perturbations.

Both address implicit adaptation claims (C76-C77, C144). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting these are explicitly labeled as speculation by authors. Peer Reviewer 1 questions whether evidence supports exclusive implicit control and suggests removing 'implicit' from title/abstract, indicating similar uncertainty about this interpretation.

Both address gradual vs. abrupt perturbation comparison (C73-C75). OpenEval finds the control data appropriately documented despite smaller sample size in abrupt condition. Peer Reviewer 1 notes 'there is no clear comparison between gradual and abrupt sessions,' suggesting the comparison could be strengthened.

Both address minimal intervention principle interpretation (C67, C139-C140, C147, C163-C168). OpenEval notes conflicting interpretations within the manuscript (UNCERTAIN). Peer reviewers request more discussion of why both perturbation types drive adaptation and how this relates to internal model predictions.

Both address generalizability limitations (C113). OpenEval finds the acknowledgment appropriate given the specific configuration tested (SUPPORTED). Peer Reviewer 3 and editor explicitly raise concerns about limited generalizability, requesting future work examining different configurations (UNCERTAIN).

Minimal overlap. OpenEval R13 addresses extensive background and novelty claims (C1-C36, C107-C128), finding them well-supported. Peer R1 focuses on task design praise but shares only C127 regarding novelty. Both find the conceptual framework and task innovation well-established.

OpenEval R9 addresses Experiment 3 design and predictions (C96-C100, C193-C195), finding them logically derived and clearly stated. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses the experimental design rationale, though peer reviewers accepted the results (see peer R6).

OpenEval R15 addresses literature contextualization (C133-C135, C141-C143), finding comparisons to prior work appropriate. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these literature comparisons.

OpenEval R17 addresses distinction from previous 'task-irrelevant' work (C150-C154), finding the conceptual clarification important and well-supported. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this distinction, though it relates to the novelty praised in peer R1.

OpenEval R18 addresses Experiment 3 interpretations about interaction and dual optimization (C159, C161-C162), finding them logical though interpretive. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these Experiment 3 interpretations.

OpenEval R19 addresses data analysis methods (C196-C202), finding them appropriate with minor suggestions for more detail on multiple comparisons. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses methodological details.
